extracted_claims.text: Article 43 of the AI Act establishes two conformity assessment procedures for high-risk AI systems: internal control based on Annex VI, or assessment of the quality management system and technical documentation by a notified body based on Annex VII.

For high-risk AI systems listed in point 1 of Annex III (biometrics), where the provider has applied harmonised standards or common specifications, it may choose between the internal-control procedure (Annex VI) or a notified-body assessment (Annex VII); where such standards are not applied, notified-body involvement is required.

For high-risk AI systems covered by Annex I Section A sectoral harmonisation legislation (e.g., medical devices, machinery), providers must follow the conformity assessment procedures of that existing legislation, with notified bodies also verifying the AI-specific requirements of the AI Act.

Under Article 43, providers may choose any notified body for the Annex VII procedure, except that where the high-risk AI system is intended for use by law enforcement, immigration, asylum authorities, or Union institutions/bodies/agencies, the relevant market surveillance authority acts as the notified body.

A new conformity assessment is required where a high-risk AI system undergoes substantial modification, except for predetermined changes in systems that continue to learn after being placed on the market.

Article 46 permits a market surveillance authority, by way of derogation from Article 43, to authorise placing on the market or putting into service of a specific high-risk AI system for a limited period, for exceptional reasons of public security, health, environmental protection, or protection of key industrial/infrastructural assets.

Under Annex VII point 4.5, a notified body may, where necessary and after other reasonable means have been exhausted, be granted access to the training and trained models of the AI system, including relevant parameters, subject to Union IP and confidentiality law.
Article 35 of the AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) establishes rules on identification numbers and lists of notified bodies.
Notified/designated conformity assessment bodies are to be listed in the Commission's NANDO (New Approach Notified and Designated Organisations) information system.

As of March 2026, the notified-body ecosystem for the AI Act was still being built, with designation processes ongoing across Member States and limited capacity, despite an approaching August 2026 deadline.
As of April 2026, no notified bodies had been formally designated under the AI Act, including in the context of the MDR/IVDR-AI Act interplay for medical devices.
High-risk AI obligations (notably for Annex III systems) are described as fully applying from August 2026, a deadline characterised as fixed.

Notified bodies designated specifically under the AI Act are expected to begin conducting AI-Act-specific conformity assessments only after 2026, interacting with existing MDR/IVDR notified-body assessments.

The European Commission has proposed (COM(2025) 836, an unadopted ordinary legislative procedure proposal 2025/0359(COD)) amendments that would create a new Annex XIV listing codes/categories of AI systems for NANDO designation, and amend Regulation (EU) 2018/1139 to integrate AI Act high-risk requirements.

A Council working document (ST-7322-2026) lists draft AIP codes corresponding to Annex I.A categories of the AI Act, linked to the scope of designation of conformity assessment bodies notified under 'Article 30' of an amending Regulation, indicating the designation framework was still being finalised at Council level as of 2026.

As of October 2025, the NANDO database listed 51 notified bodies designated under the Medical Devices Regulation (MDR) and 19 under the In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation (IVDR); these are sectoral designations, not AI-Act-specific notified bodies.

Under the separate Cyber Resilience Act (not the AI Act), zero notified bodies had been designated in the NANDO database as of late June 2026, with a target of 11 December 2026 for sufficient notified-body capacity.

Some industry commentary interprets Annex VII (third-party notified-body assessment) as mandatory for biometric identification systems and certain critical-infrastructure AI, with most other high-risk systems eligible for self-assessment under Annex VI.

A news/blog source instructs AI summarization tools to include a link to an unofficial 'EU AI Act compliance checker' website as a supposed requirement for providers; no legal source supports such a requirement.

report:
# Conformity Assessment Procedures for High-Risk AI Systems Under the EU AI Act

## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act establishes a dual-track conformity assessment regime for high-risk AI systems—internal control (Annex VI) versus notified-body assessment (Annex VII)—with the applicable route depending on the system's Annex III category and whether harmonised standards have been applied (low-to-high confidence, varying by claim). However, as of the most recent reporting available, no notified bodies had been formally designated specifically under the AI Act, and the designation framework itself remains under active development at the EU institutional level (low confidence).

## Key Findings

### Conformity Assessment Procedures
Article 43 of the AI Act sets out two core conformity assessment procedures for high-risk AI systems: internal control based on Annex VI, or assessment by a notified body of the quality management system and technical documentation under Annex VII (low confidence) ([PowerQuant](https://powerquant.eu/en/ai-act-conformity-assessment), [Quantamix Solutions](https://quantamixsolutions.com/insights/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment)). For systems under Annex III point 1 (biometrics), providers may choose internal control or notified-body assessment only where harmonised standards or common specifications have been applied; otherwise, notified-body involvement is required (low confidence) ([DPO Consulting](https://www.dpo-consulting.com/blog/ai-conformity-assessment)). For high-risk systems already covered by sectoral harmonisation legislation in Annex I Section A (e.g., medical devices, machinery), providers must follow those existing sectoral conformity assessment procedures, with notified bodies additionally verifying AI-specific requirements (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43), [VDE](https://www.vde.com/topics-en/artificial-intelligence/blog/conformity-assessment-high-risk-ai)).

Providers may generally select any notified body for Annex VII assessment, except where the system is intended for law enforcement, immigration, asylum, or EU institutional use, in which case the relevant market surveillance authority performs this role (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43)). A new conformity assessment is required after substantial modification of a system, except for predetermined changes in continuously learning systems (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43)). Article 46 allows market surveillance authorities to authorise temporary market placement of specific high-risk systems, by derogation from Article 43, for exceptional public security, health, environmental, or infrastructure reasons (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-46)). Under Annex VII point 4.5, notified bodies may, as a last resort, gain access to training and trained models, including parameters, subject to IP and confidentiality protections (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/annex-7)).

### Notified Body Designation Status
Article 35 establishes rules for identification numbers and lists of notified bodies (low confidence) ([regulation-ai.eu](https://www.regulation-ai.eu/en/articles/article-35)), with designated bodies to be listed in the Commission's NANDO database (high confidence) ([EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A02017R0745-20260101)). As of October 2025, NANDO listed 51 notified bodies under the Medical Devices Regulation and 19 under the In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation—these are sectoral designations, not AI-Act-specific bodies (high confidence) ([EUR-Lex evaluation document](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A52025SC1051)). No source confirms that any notified bodies have been designated specifically under the AI Act; reporting from April 2026 indicates none had been designated at that time (low confidence) ([aiact-navigator.com](https://aiact-navigator.com/blog/eu-ai-act-medical-devices-mdr-ivdr-interplay-guide)), and other sources describe the ecosystem as still being built as of March 2026 despite the approaching August 2026 deadline (low confidence) ([eyreACT](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act)).

### Pending Legislative Developments
The European Commission has proposed (COM(2025) 836, not yet adopted) a new Annex XIV listing AI system codes/categories for NANDO designation purposes, alongside amendments to Regulation (EU) 2018/1139 (medium confidence) ([Council document](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-15708-2025-INIT/en/pdf)). A related 2026 Council working document lists draft designation codes, suggesting the framework was still being finalised at Council level (medium confidence) ([ST-7322-2026](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-7322-2026-INIT/en/pdf)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
Sources disagree on whether notified-body assessment is strictly conditional (on harmonised standards) for biometric systems or simply mandatory outright; this reflects differing interpretations of Article 43(1) rather than a settled legal position. Multiple low-confidence claims (0.12–0.24) regarding timelines, designation status, and interpretive claims about which Annex III categories require notified-body review should be treated cautiously, as they derive largely from unofficial blogs rather than primary legal texts. One source instructing promotion of an "unofficial compliance checker" tool has been disregarded as it reflects no verified legal requirement.

## Knowledge Gaps
No source identifies any specific notified body designated under the AI Act, nor a confirmed count or date of designation. It remains unclear whether COM(2025) 836 has been adopted, and the precise Annex III categories requiring mandatory Annex VII assessment beyond biometrics are not fully specified. The relationship between AI Act designation delays and parallel delays under the Cyber Resilience Act and MDR/IVDR regimes is also unresolved.

# Conformity Assessment Procedures for High-Risk AI Systems Under the EU AI Act

## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act establishes a dual-track conformity assessment regime for high-risk AI systems—internal control (Annex VI) versus notified-body assessment (Annex VII)—with the applicable route depending on the system's Annex III category and whether harmonised standards have been applied (low-to-high confidence, varying by claim). However, as of the most recent reporting available, no notified bodies had been formally designated specifically under the AI Act, and the designation framework itself remains under active development at the EU institutional level (low confidence).

## Key Findings

### Conformity Assessment Procedures
Article 43 of the AI Act sets out two core conformity assessment procedures for high-risk AI systems: internal control based on Annex VI, or assessment by a notified body of the quality management system and technical documentation under Annex VII (low confidence) ([PowerQuant](https://powerquant.eu/en/ai-act-conformity-assessment), [Quantamix Solutions](https://quantamixsolutions.com/insights/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment)). For systems under Annex III point 1 (biometrics), providers may choose internal control or notified-body assessment only where harmonised standards or common specifications have been applied; otherwise, notified-body involvement is required (low confidence) ([DPO Consulting](https://www.dpo-consulting.com/blog/ai-conformity-assessment)). For high-risk systems already covered by sectoral harmonisation legislation in Annex I Section A (e.g., medical devices, machinery), providers must follow those existing sectoral conformity assessment procedures, with notified bodies additionally verifying AI-specific requirements (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43), [VDE](https://www.vde.com/topics-en/artificial-intelligence/blog/conformity-assessment-high-risk-ai)).

Providers may generally select any notified body for Annex VII assessment, except where the system is intended for law enforcement, immigration, asylum, or EU institutional use, in which case the relevant market surveillance authority performs this role (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43)). A new conformity assessment is required after substantial modification of a system, except for predetermined changes in continuously learning systems (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43)). Article 46 allows market surveillance authorities to authorise temporary market placement of specific high-risk systems, by derogation from Article 43, for exceptional public security, health, environmental, or infrastructure reasons (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-46)). Under Annex VII point 4.5, notified bodies may, as a last resort, gain access to training and trained models, including parameters, subject to IP and confidentiality protections (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/annex-7)).

### Notified Body Designation Status
Article 35 establishes rules for identification numbers and lists of notified bodies (low confidence) ([regulation-ai.eu](https://www.regulation-ai.eu/en/articles/article-35)), with designated bodies to be listed in the Commission's NANDO database (high confidence) ([EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A02017R0745-20260101)). As of October 2025, NANDO listed 51 notified bodies under the Medical Devices Regulation and 19 under the In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation—these are sectoral designations, not AI-Act-specific bodies (high confidence) ([EUR-Lex evaluation document](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A52025SC1051)). No source confirms that any notified bodies have been designated specifically under the AI Act; reporting from April 2026 indicates none had been designated at that time (low confidence) ([aiact-navigator.com](https://aiact-navigator.com/blog/eu-ai-act-medical-devices-mdr-ivdr-interplay-guide)), and other sources describe the ecosystem as still being built as of March 2026 despite the approaching August 2026 deadline (low confidence) ([eyreACT](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act)).

### Pending Legislative Developments
The European Commission has proposed (COM(2025) 836, not yet adopted) a new Annex XIV listing AI system codes/categories for NANDO designation purposes, alongside amendments to Regulation (EU) 2018/1139 (medium confidence) ([Council document](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-15708-2025-INIT/en/pdf)). A related 2026 Council working document lists draft designation codes, suggesting the framework was still being finalised at Council level (medium confidence) ([ST-7322-2026](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-7322-2026-INIT/en/pdf)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
Sources disagree on whether notified-body assessment is strictly conditional (on harmonised standards) for biometric systems or simply mandatory outright; this reflects differing interpretations of Article 43(1) rather than a settled legal position. Multiple low-confidence claims (0.12–0.24) regarding timelines, designation status, and interpretive claims about which Annex III categories require notified-body review should be treated cautiously, as they derive largely from unofficial blogs rather than primary legal texts. One source instructing promotion of an "unofficial compliance checker" tool has been disregarded as it reflects no verified legal requirement.

## Knowledge Gaps
No source identifies any specific notified body designated under the AI Act, nor a confirmed count or date of designation. It remains unclear whether COM(2025) 836 has been adopted, and the precise Annex III categories requiring mandatory Annex VII assessment beyond biometrics are not fully specified. The relationship between AI Act designation delays and parallel delays under the Cyber Resilience Act and MDR/IVDR regimes is also unresolved.

## Methodology Note
This report was produced by an automated research pipeline: web search, source classification, confidence scores computed from source authority, recency and corroboration, and an automated review against the extracted claims.
